name: Executive Order of July 13, 1880 (Fort Berthold Reservation boundaries)
promises: This was an executive order, not a treaty; the nations did not sign it. It changed the reservation the three nations had kept from the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty, which recognised their territory south and west of the Missouri River between the Heart and Yellowstone rivers.
The order added a tract north-east of the Missouri to the reservation in exchange for Fort Laramie treaty lands south of the river (as the ICC described it in Docket 350-A).

breaches.what: By executive order the President took from the Fort Berthold Reservation lands south of the Missouri that the nations held under the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty, giving land north-east of the river in exchange. The Indian Claims Commission records the exchange; the nations' claim for the difference in value went to trial.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Executive Order of July 13, 1880, as described by the Indian Claims Commission in Docket 350-A (1968) and Docket 350-D (1976)

breaches.what: Under a 1920 jurisdictional act the nations sued for the lands taken from their Fort Laramie reservation by the executive orders of 1868, 1870 and 1880. The Court of Claims found 11,424,512.76 acres taken and 1,578,325.83 added under those orders, held the nations entitled to just compensation for the net 9,846,186.93 acres 'for which no compensation was received', and valued them at 50 cents an acre.

breaches.what: The nations' claim for the difference in value between the lands lost and the lands added by the 1870 and 1880 executive orders was tried on value and then settled by a $3,200,000 compromise judgment, without a finding.

breaches.what: The MHA Nation says the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty recognised over 12 million acres as its homeland and that later treaties, executive orders and Acts of Congress reduced this to less than 3 million.
breaches.whoFoundIt: MHA Nation (Three Affiliated Tribes), History page

compensation: None at the time. The Court of Claims (71 Ct. Cl. 308, 1930) awarded 50 cents an acre for the net 9,846,186.93 acres taken under the 1868, 1870 and 1880 orders. Docket 350-D, for the difference in value between the lands lost and the lands added, was compromised for $3,200,000 in 1976.
today: The north-east tract added in 1880 was ceded in turn under the 1886 agreement ratified in 1891 (see cession-1891-03-03-gros-ventre-mandan).

nationVoice.summary: Counts the executive orders and federal acts after 1851 as the steps by which over 12 million recognised acres became less than 3 million.

openQuestions: The text of the 1880 order (1 Kappler 883) was not opened; textUrl points to the ICC opinion that describes it.

Consent: no source opened says the nations consented to the 1880 order, and the 1930 Court of Claims judgment, as the Commission describes it, treats the lands as taken from them without compensation. The 1930 opinion itself (71 Ct. Cl. 308) was not opened.

Audit 2026-11-08: added a court-ruling breach, Fort Berthold Indians v. United States, 71 Ct. Cl. 308 (1930), from the Commission's 1970 Docket 350-D opinion (23 Ind. Cl. Comm. 236), which records that the Court of Claims held the lands taken under the 1868, 1870 and 1880 orders compensable and found no compensation had been received; landTaken and compensation filled from the same opinion. The status rests on this ruling, not on the executive order alone.
landTaken: The Court of Claims found 11,424,512.76 acres taken from the Fort Berthold reservation under the executive orders of 1868, 1870 and 1880, and 1,578,325.83 acres added under the orders of 1870, 1880 and 1892, a net 9,846,186.93 acres taken without compensation (Fort Berthold Indians v. United States, 71 Ct. Cl. 308 (1930), as quoted in 23 Ind. Cl. Comm. 236). The Commission's table gives 1,378,645.83 acres added by the 1880 order; the acreage taken by the 1880 order alone is not legible in the scan.
